source.title: The Computational Limits of Deep Learning
source.authors: Neil C. Thompson; Kristjan H. Greenewald; Keeheon Lee; Gabriel F. Manso

record.file_problem: No apparent garbling, truncation, or document mismatch.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own regressions of benchmark performance against compute and argues that estimates can differ with the scaling approach and functional form. This refines the scope of scaling claims, but does not test language-model held-out cross-entropy or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.gate_note: The paper studies historical benchmark performance against network operations or hardware burden, not held-out language-model loss against parameter count, tokens, or compute. Its benchmark regressions and functional-form comparisons bear on V6 and V7. Comparisons to results from other papers and cited individual compression results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: This is a cross-paper meta-analysis of benchmark error against training compute, mostly for vision models and task-specific NLP models. Each regression pools models from different papers and years, so the compute slope mixes scaling with algorithmic innovation. It does not measure held-out language-model pretraining loss. It does not measure downstream performance of a language-model family as scale or pretraining loss changes. It does not run controlled scale sweeps. This is a related but different construct (field-level progress versus compute), so its findings go under fits_no_version. It cites Kaplan et al. and compares its own estimates with within-model studies only qualitatively. No verdicts are given.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right, but the emphasis is off. The authors conclude that benchmark progress across many deep-learning applications has relied strongly on increases in compute, following polynomial (power-law) dependence. Extrapolating these trends makes further progress economically, technically and environmentally unsustainable. Continued progress therefore needs dramatically more computationally efficient methods, either within deep learning or by moving to other ML approaches. Their field-level 'scaling up' estimates are argued to be more reliable than within-model 'scaling down' studies.
record.recipe_differences: Historical meta-analysis of performance and compute across benchmark papers, rather than controlled language-model scaling experiments measuring held-out cross-entropy over parameters, tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: ImageNet estimates vary across specifications, including adding a year trend and using a 10% quantile regression; the paper argues scaling-up and scaling-down analyses have different interpretations. Polynomial forms are preferred, but exponential fits are also described as plausible.

fits_no_version.finding: Across models from many papers, benchmark error falls roughly as a power of training compute. ImageNet implied factor is about 12 (network operations) and 10.8 (hardware burden). COCO is about 16, SQuAD 10.5, CoNLL 37.2 (weak fit). The quantile regression of the most efficient models gives a similar factor (11.9).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Field-level state-of-the-art benchmark error across successive published models scales polynomially with training compute, mixing model scaling with algorithmic progress.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding a year trend raises ImageNet R2 from 0.712 to 0.822 and shifts the implied factor to 15.5. The authors report 3 years of algorithmic progress as equivalent to 10× compute. An exponential form fits less well (R2 0.622) but is called roughly equivalent for extrapolation, giving very different projections.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Estimates of compute dependence from historical benchmark data depend on specification (time trend, functional form), and alternative forms with similar fit diverge greatly on extrapolation.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors argue that scaling-down studies of single model families (e.g. ResNet, NASNet) overstate how well models scale compared with field-level scaling-up estimates.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within-model scaling exponents estimated by shrinking a model can overstate the gains from scaling up.

record.problems: The paper says many source papers omit or incompletely report computation details, and notes data scarcity, inaccurate data, inconsistent reporting, and uncertainty in hardware performance. Some regressions cover few observations; the CoNLL result has low explanatory power and is called preliminary. The study is observational and compares models across papers, rather than controlling model, data, schedule, or architecture.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted from the study's own relevant regressions. Results cited from other studies, including the individual scaling estimates compared in Section 4 and cited compression results in Section 5, are not rows because they are not results produced by this study.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss sweep over parameters, tokens or compute.
No small-run fits extrapolated to larger runs. Table 3 extrapolations are of field-level benchmark trends, with no observed outcome to check against.
No shape or architecture comparison at fixed parameters.
No controlled power-law loss scaling in other modalities. Vision results are cross-paper benchmark-error regressions.
No language-model downstream performance as a function of model scale or pretraining loss.
No comparison of fitting choices for LM loss laws: parameter counting, schedule, data, or compute-optimal split.

missing.what: Implied polynomial scaling factor with year trend: 15.5 (95% CI 13.3–18.5), changed from 12.1 without it.

Polynomial versus exponential extrapolations of compute, CO2 and cost needed to reach target error rates on four benchmarks. The two forms are described as roughly equivalent fits but extrapolate very differently (e.g. ImageNet 1% error: 10^33 vs 10^92 flops).
Supplementary tests of alternative functional forms for the hardware-burden regressions: polynomial fits best, exponential plausible. No numbers are given in the text.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V6 and V7 links were overreach. V6 concerns downstream predictability of language models with scale or pretraining loss. These are cross-paper regressions of benchmark error, mostly for vision and task-specific NLP models. The compute slope is confounded with innovation over time. Kaplan et al. appears only in comparison tables and qualitative agreement statements ('notionally agree with the power law growths'). I classify the study as discussing the claim, not testing it.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out language-model pretraining cross-entropy sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No test of small-run fits predicting much larger runs.
No fixed-compute optimization of parameter and token counts.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.
The paper covers several application domains, but does not test whether the language-model loss power law carries over to other modalities or training regimes.

Tests benchmark performance against compute, not performance against language-model pretraining loss or parameter count; the study does not isolate downstream performance of pretrained language models.

Tests choices of scaling direction and functional form in benchmark-performance-versus-compute analyses. It does not test parameter-counting choices, training schedules, data choices, or compute-optimal allocation, and does not directly establish that curves bend away from a power law.

rows.subject: ImageNet benchmark model set (aggregate across models)
rows.operation_detail: Regressed ImageNet top-1 error against network operations across literature models.

conditions.value: Network Operations, normalized relative to 2012 AlexNet
OLS, log10(Top 1 error) against log10(Network Operations)

rows.measure: Performance-versus-compute regression; implied polynomial scaling factor for computation with performance.
rows.value: Slope coefficient -0.082; implied computation scaling factor 12.1; 95% confidence interval 10.6–14.1; p-value < 0.01; R2 0.712.
rows.uncertainty: Coefficient standard error 0.006; 95% confidence interval for implied factor 10.6–14.1.
rows.note: Aggregate regression over models in the literature, not a single model or a controlled scale sweep. The text says compute is a statistically significant predictor and explains 71% of ImageNet performance variance.
rows.check: ImageNet error versus network operations across vision models from many papers. These are not language models, and the measure is not loss. The fit is field-level, not a controlled sweep. It does not measure what V6 names.

rows.subject: ImageNet benchmark model set (aggregate across models)
rows.operation_detail: Added a year trend to the ImageNet performance-versus-network-operations regression.
rows.measure: Performance-versus-compute regression with an algorithmic-change proxy.
rows.value: R2 0.822; text says explanatory power rises by 11%, three years of algorithm improvement are equivalent to a 10× increase in compute, and the power-law relationship remains.
rows.uncertainty: Table reports standard errors 0.005 for the compute coefficient and 0.003 for the year coefficient; p<0.01 for both.
rows.note: Aggregate historical regression. This specification changes the estimated slope as well as the explanatory power; the text gives the compute-equivalent time trend.
rows.check: Field-level ImageNet regression with a year trend. The value omits that the implied scaling factor shifts from 12.1 to 15.5 (CI 13.3–18.5) once the trend is added. The fit-choice sensitivity concerns benchmark-error regressions, not published LM scaling laws (V7).

rows.subject: ImageNet benchmark model set (aggregate across models)
rows.operation_detail: Estimated performance-versus-compute relation using quantile regression for the 10% most efficient models.
rows.measure: Implied polynomial scaling factor for computation with performance.
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence interval 10.6–13.5; coefficient standard error 0.005 in Table 2(a).
rows.note: The paper says the estimate for the 10% most efficient models shows a similar dependence on compute.
rows.check: 10% quantile regression on cross-paper ImageNet models. Same construct mismatch as R1. It is a robustness check that gives a similar factor (11.9 vs 12.1).

rows.subject: ImageNet benchmark model set (aggregate across models)
rows.operation_detail: Regressed ImageNet performance against hardware burden across literature models.
rows.measure: Performance-versus-hardware-burden regression; implied polynomial scaling factor.
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence interval 9.5–12.3; Table 2(b) coefficient standard error 0.006, p<0.01.
rows.check: ImageNet error versus hardware burden across vision models. Not language-model downstream scaling.

rows.subject: MS COCO benchmark model set (aggregate across models)
rows.operation_detail: Regressed object-detection performance against hardware burden across literature models.
rows.measure: Performance-versus-hardware-burden regression; implied polynomial scaling factor.
rows.value: Table 2(b): implied factor 16.0, 95% confidence interval 13.0–21.3, R2 0.809. Prose reports a dependence of 17.1.
rows.uncertainty: Table 2(b) 95% confidence interval 13.0–21.3; coefficient standard error 0.012, p<0.01.
rows.note: Aggregate regression. The prose and table report different implied factors; both are retained as stated.
rows.check: MS COCO detection models across papers, with only 20 observations. Not language models. Hardware burden was partly converted from network operations using the ImageNet conversion model. The prose (17.1) and table (16.0) disagree, as the record notes.

rows.subject: SQuAD 1.1 benchmark model set (aggregate across models)
rows.operation_detail: Regressed question-answering performance against hardware burden across literature models.
rows.measure: Performance-versus-hardware-burden regression; implied polynomial scaling factor.
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence interval 8.3–14.3; coefficient standard error 0.012, p<0.01.
rows.check: SQuAD 1.1 models across papers, with only 12 observations. The models are task-trained and heterogeneous, not one LM family scaled. The regression is field-level performance versus hardware burden, not V6's relation.

rows.subject: CoNLL 2003 benchmark model set (aggregate across models)
rows.operation_detail: Regressed named-entity-recognition performance against hardware burden across literature models.
rows.measure: Performance-versus-hardware-burden regression; implied polynomial scaling factor.
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence interval 20.4–200; coefficient standard error 0.010, p<0.05.
rows.note: The paper says hardware burden rises substantially for relatively small outcome improvements and calls the result preliminary because the model explains only 43% of the variance.
rows.check: CoNLL 2003 regression with 12 observations and R2 0.43, which the authors call preliminary. Same construct mismatch. The 'partial' state is not meaningful against any version.

rows.subject: WMT 2014 machine-translation benchmark model set (aggregate; language directions not separated in the reported statement)
rows.operation_detail: Examined the association between hardware burden and machine-translation performance.
rows.measure: Reported compute-performance association and ability to estimate its slope.
rows.value: The text reports a correlation between compute and performance, but says there was insufficient variation in compute to estimate the slope reliably.
rows.note: The statement does not give separate results for EN-FR and EN-DE.
rows.check: Qualitative statement only: a correlation exists but there was too little compute variation to estimate a slope. No value can be read.

rows.subject: ImageNet benchmark model set (aggregate across models)
rows.operation_detail: Compared polynomial and exponential functional forms for ImageNet performance versus network operations.
rows.measure: Relative fit of alternative performance-versus-compute functional forms.
rows.value: The exponential specification is statistically significant but has lower explanatory power (R2 0.622); the authors retain the polynomial specification as preferred.
rows.uncertainty: Table reports standard errors 0.003 for the exponential specification's slope and p<0.01.
rows.note: The text also says supplementary hardware-burden analyses find polynomial models fit best, while exponential models remain plausible; it does not give the supplementary estimates here.
rows.check: Compares polynomial and exponential forms for field-level ImageNet error versus compute (R2 0.712 vs 0.622). It concerns the functional form of benchmark-progress regressions, not LM loss laws.

rows.subject: Across-model benchmark scaling analyses discussed by the authors
rows.operation_detail: Argued that scaling up a field's performance and scaling down a state-of-the-art model are not symmetric ways to estimate scaling.

conditions.value: ImageNet examples and comparisons discussed in Section 4

rows.measure: Authors' stated interpretation of how scaling approach changes the meaning and apparent strength of a scaling estimate.
rows.value: The authors argue that scaling down can make rapid performance deterioration look like good scaling, whereas scaling up measures improvement in the field; they use this to qualify comparisons among published scaling estimates.
rows.note: This is the authors' argument about interpretation and methodology, not a new row of results from the cited studies.
rows.check: Should not be a row. It is the authors' conceptual argument (scaling up vs scaling down), illustrated with results cited from ResNet, NASNet and EfficientNet. It is not a result produced by this study.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
